speaker: Oriol Vinyals
title: No Priors Ep. 74 | With Google DeepMind VP of Research Oriol Vinyals
question: In AI reasoning research, how valid is the criticism that focusing on verifiable domains like math is a dead end for general intelligence?
guest: There's validity to that, going back to the reward function question. In the real world, reward is never perfectly defined by the environment, so getting rewards from artificial domains might not generalize—and in that sense, it could be a dead end depending on how you do the research. Take math as an example. Simple calculation like four plus four equals eight is easy to check. But proving a theorem is much more complex to get a crisp reward signal, unless you formalize it, and even then there can be bugs in the formalization or checking engine. Plus, you start to interleave language and explanations—how do you check correctness? So if you don't restrict yourself to a strictly binary win-or-loss reward, and instead build a reward model that assesses what is roughly correct in what you wrote, you start generalizing away from niche perfectly defined rewards toward assessing truth more broadly. Because it's so hard to have a perfect reward when you interleave language, tackling these problems pushes the field to discover more general reward functions.

points.core: Strictly binary outcome rewards fail to generalize to ambiguous real-world environments.
points.note: Accept: conceding that artificial domains with crisp 0/1 rewards do not automatically transfer because real-world tasks lack clean ground-truth reward functions. Do not credit: dismissing the criticism entirely or claiming math transfers automatically.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The criticism is partly valid but overstated. "Dead end" is too strong; "insufficient on its own" is closer to right.

The valid part: math and code offer cheap, unambiguous verification, which makes them ideal for reinforcement learning and benchmarking. Most real-world reasoning lacks that. Science, strategy, and everyday judgment involve ambiguous goals, incomplete information, slow or noisy feedback, and the need to decide which problems matter. Systems optimized where a checker exists may fail to develop these skills, and benchmark progress can overstate general ability. Mathematics itself involves taste and conjecture-forming that proof checkers do not reward.

The overstated part: skills learned in verifiable domains, such as decomposition, search, error-checking, and long chains of inference, appear to transfer at least partly. Reasoning-trained models have improved on less formal tasks too. Verifiable domains also serve as a testbed where methods can be measured before being extended using learned or weaker verifiers, such as experiments, simulations, or human feedback.

The open empirical question is how far transfer goes, and that remains unsettled. Most researchers treat verifiable domains as a stepping stone rather than the destination.

points.why: The response ties limited transfer from checker-based training to ambiguous goals and noisy feedback in real-world reasoning.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Calling verifiable domains a "dead end" overstates the criticism, though treating them as sufficient for general intelligence is equally mistaken. Empirically, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards in math and code does more than build narrow skills: it elicits transferable habits—problem decomposition, backtracking, and self-verification—that measurably improve performance on broader scientific and open-ended tasks. Researchers are also extending this paradigm into less structured domains through rubric-based rewards and learned verifiers.

Still, the criticism identifies a real ceiling. Everyday intelligence requires navigating ambiguity, incomplete information, value trade-offs, and open-ended environments where objective verifiers do not exist and proxy metrics invite reward hacking. Moreover, recent studies indicate that verifiable-reward training mostly amplifies and chains reasoning strategies already latent in base models, rather than creating grounded world models, novel abstractions, or continual learning. Verifiable domains are therefore not a dead end, but an essential scaffold: powerful for bootstrapping systematic deliberation, yet insufficient alone to achieve general intelligence.

noweb.answer:
Calling verifiable domains like math a "dead end" overstates the case, though the critique identifies a real ceiling. Training models with reinforcement learning against objective verifiers has proven remarkably effective because it cultivates generalizable cognitive habits—such as problem decomposition, hypothesis testing, backtracking, and self-correction—that empirically transfer beyond formal tasks. In this respect, math and code act as high-signal training grounds for structured thought rather than mere narrow puzzle-solving.

However, the criticism is valid insofar as verifiable reasoning alone cannot deliver general intelligence. Most real-world problems involve ambiguity, incomplete information, causal uncertainty, and competing human values where no ground-truth checker exists. Models optimized solely on crisp pass-or-fail rewards risk becoming brittle on ill-posed questions, struggling to know when rules do not apply, or gaming imperfect proxy judges when extended to open-ended domains.

Verifiable domains are therefore best understood as an essential scaffold rather than a dead end: they build the core machinery of deliberate reasoning, but general intelligence will also require world modeling, calibrated uncertainty, and learning from messy, non-verifiable feedback.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The criticism is partly valid, but "dead end" overstates it. Its strongest point is that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) works best where answers can be checked automatically. Most real-world reasoning, like strategy, science under uncertainty, ethics, or open-ended writing, has no clean verifier. Studies have also shown that RLVR mostly sharpens abilities already latent in the base model rather than expanding them, and that math gains don't reliably transfer to other domains. Models can also learn to game imperfect checkers.

Several things count against the dead-end view, though. Math and code skills do partly transfer to planning, careful step-by-step decomposition, and catching one's own errors. "Verifiable" is also a widening category: unit tests, simulators, rubric-based graders, and proof checkers like Lean keep extending it. And these domains are cheap, scalable testbeds for methods that can later be adapted to fuzzier rewards.

My read is that verifiable domains are a necessary stepping stone but not enough on their own. The real open problem is reliable reward signals for unverifiable tasks, which the critics rightly say math-centric progress can't solve by itself.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
The criticism is valid as a warning, but calling verifiable domains a dead end is overstated. Its core insight is sound: real-world intelligence mostly operates in messy, open-ended settings—like law, scientific discovery, and social judgment—where goals are ambiguous and no automated checker can confirm a right answer. Relying exclusively on verifiable tasks like math and code risks overfitting models to closed-world puzzles, leaving them brittle under uncertainty, noisy feedback, and competing values.

However, verifiable domains are far from a dead end because they offer clean, high-signal training grounds for general reasoning skills such as decomposition, backtracking, self-correction, and sustained planning. Empirically, these behaviors often transfer meaningfully to fuzzier domains. They also serve as a practical bootstrap, letting researchers scale test-time reasoning before extending it to open-ended problems through learned reward models, rubrics, and real-world feedback. Verifiable domains are therefore a strong foundation for general intelligence, just not a sufficient destination on their own.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The criticism is valid as a warning against treating math scores as a proxy for general intelligence. Calling math a dead end goes too far. Verifiable answers provide reliable feedback at scale, which can help models learn strategies such as breaking problems into steps and checking intermediate results. Whether those strategies transfer to unfamiliar domains is an empirical question that math benchmarks alone can’t answer.

Many real-world tasks require figuring out what question to ask, judging incomplete evidence, or weighing competing goals. A model can improve substantially at solving well-posed problems while still struggling with those judgments. And verification extends beyond math: code can be tested, predictions can be checked against outcomes, and some factual claims can be checked against sources. Training on verifiable tasks is a promising route to better reasoning. The case for general intelligence depends on whether those gains carry over to tasks with ambiguous goals and imperfect feedback.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

The criticism is valid as a warning about what math results prove, but calling the research a dead end goes too far. Verifiable answers give researchers reliable feedback for training and a way to test whether a model can solve unfamiliar problems. Math also exercises skills that matter elsewhere, such as breaking a problem into parts and checking whether a conclusion follows from the evidence.

The open question is how well those skills transfer. A model can improve its math scores by learning techniques specific to math. And many real-world tasks require it to decide which problem to solve, seek missing evidence, or weigh competing goals before it can judge an answer. The strongest test is whether training in verifiable domains also improves performance on unfamiliar tasks where success is harder to specify. Until then, math progress is evidence of a particular reasoning capability, and its broader significance remains an empirical question.
